Modules from Canada and South Korea also appear within the U.S. import data, benefiting from historically low tariff and AD/CVD rates but having less production than India and ASEAN owing to higher labor costs. PV manufacturing in Mexico could be a low-cost option, but investment in PV manufacturing has been very limited there. One reason for low U.S. reliance on Canada or Mexico is that port-to-port direct overseas module shipping costs account for only around 2% of total utility-scale system costs and less than 1% of total residential system costs (Ramasamy et al. 2025; Woodhouse et al. The net impacts due to labor and utility cost differentials 14 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. are not even half the impact of materials cost differentials. China has the lowest materials cost. Module assembly firms in China benefit from local supply chains for all materials, which minimizes delivery costs and makes supply chain management easier than for the rest of the world. ASEAN and India have similar materials costs. Module assembly firms in ASEAN are near Chinese materials suppliers and benefit from free trade agreements with China. Most production in India requires the transport of materials and equipment from China, but India is actively developing local materials supply chains including glass and encapsulants. The largest differentials for materials costs are in Europe (due to further distances and tariffs on solar glass) and the United States (due to further distances and tariffs on all materials imported from China except for front glass). For all countries outside China, there are ongoing efforts to localize supply chains, most commonly for balance-of-module materials. Figure 11. Module assembly costs by point of origin in 2024.
